episode_title: Episode 258: Dr. Eric Block - Dr. Block's Deep Dive on Class 2 Composites

real_qa.q: What is Dr. Eric Block's workflow for Class 2 composite restorations using the two band, one wedge, one ring technique?
real_qa.r: Dr. Block uses a two-band, one-wedge, one-ring technique for back-to-back Class 2 composites. He places two bands facing opposite directions, secures them with a medium-sized wedge using cotton pliers, applies one ring to contour both bands around the teeth, then restores with MicroPrime bonding followed by flowable composite layers and bulk fill composite. This technique allows him to complete two teeth in approximately 30 minutes and provides predictable proximal contacts and contours.
real_qa.requete: Class 2 composite two band one wedge technique

real_qa.q: What is the endo-ice test protocol Dr. Eric Block uses to verify anesthesia before drilling?
real_qa.r: Dr. Block's rule is 'no pass through the icy, no drilling.' His assistant takes a small piece of cotton, saturates it with endo-ice to make it extremely cold, and places it on the tooth's buccal, lingual, occlusal, and fractured areas. If the patient feels any cold sensation, they are not numb and he does not take a burr to the tooth. If coldness is still felt on lower molars after initial nerve block, he administers additional doses with buccal infiltration and potentially a Tuttle numb interosseous technique.

real_qa.q: What anesthesia protocol does Dr. Eric Block use for lower molars versus upper teeth and lower non-molar teeth?
real_qa.r: For upper teeth and lower non-molar teeth, Dr. Block gives a buccal infiltration of Septocaine and tests with ice. For lower molars, he uses an inferior alveolar nerve block with a long needle, making sure to hit bone and redirect the needle as learned in dental school. He typically tells patients lower molar anesthesia requires more than one dose. If patients still feel cold after the nerve block and buccal infiltrations, he uses a Tuttle numb interosseous technique with either Septocaine or Carbocaine.
real_qa.requete: lower molar anesthesia inferior alveolar nerve block

real_qa.q: How does Dr. Eric Block organize his operatory setup and instrument trays to streamline composite procedures?
real_qa.r: Dr. Block keeps color-coded trays and carts in each operatory organized the same way: the top drawer contains anesthetic supplies, the second drawer holds flowable composites, bonding agents, MicroPrime tips, light, brushes, and bands. He uses blue trays for composites and crowns, red for removable, and orange for endo. He documents his preferred burr and instrument setup with photos stored in Flomo software so assistants know exactly what he needs without asking.

real_qa.q: What timing does Dr. Eric Block allocate for completing Class 2 composite restorations?
real_qa.r: For two teeth, Dr. Block typically schedules 30 minutes. For lower molars, he allocates 40 minutes to allow extra time for anesthesia, which sometimes requires more than one dose. For three or four fillings, he schedules approximately one hour.

real_quote: My rule is no pass through the icy, no drilling. I do not take a burr to a tooth unless they pass the endo ice test.
key_stats: 30 minutes: typical appointment time for two back-to-back Class 2 composite restorations
40 minutes: appointment time allocated for lower molar composites due to additional anesthesia requirements
5 minutes: waiting time after administering Novocaine before testing anesthesia
3 seconds: curing time with modern high-speed LED curing lights for bonding agent and composite layers
6 burrs used for composite procedures in Dr. Block's standard setup
